setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small village of a square, a manor, an inn, a greenhouse, a church vestry and a doctor's surgery. Edmund Vale of Vale Manor is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

rules.text: The manor lies four minutes from the square; the greenhouse three minutes beyond the manor.
The study strongbox has only two keys: one on Edmund's watch chain, the other held by the estate solicitor.
When two people face each other, a swing with the right hand lands on the other person's left side, and a swing with the left hand lands on their right.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed and guarded; courteous but says little, quietly deflecting private matters. Speaks briefly.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She manages the manor and has asked that its private affairs remain private.

people.name: Rowan Pike
people.voice: A plain-spoken working man; blunt and practical, short sentences, no flourishes.
people.public: The manor’s groundskeeper. His bandaged hand and green coat have become subjects of village conversation.

people.name: Silas Voss
people.voice: A precise, careful solicitor; measured and a touch formal, but concise — never rambling.
people.public: A precise, courteous solicitor who keeps an office in the vestry. He handled Edmund’s estate accounts.

people.name: Ada Finch
people.voice: A warm, chatty innkeeper; colloquial and quick to share impressions, though she runs on a little.
people.public: The Rook & Lantern’s proprietor. She knows everyone’s habits and is certain she saw something useful last night.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Measured and clinical; direct and concise, stays to what she observed.
people.public: Methodical and direct. She examined Edmund’s body and treated a patient at the greenhouse last night.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A plain, gruff country constable; terse and matter-of-fact, everyday speech — never bureaucratic or long-winded.
people.public: Bell has secured the manor and asked you to investigate. He will hear an accusation when you can explain it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.public: Master of Vale Manor, found dead the morning the investigation begins.

objects.name: Estate account ledger
objects.desc: The bound ledger of Vale estate accounts, kept by the solicitor.

objects.name: Strongbox key
objects.desc: One of two keys to the study strongbox.

objects.name: Brass paperweight
objects.desc: A heavy brass paperweight from Edmund's desk.

objects.name: Inn bill
objects.desc: A pencilled supper bill on the spike behind the Rook's bar.

objects.name: Vestry hat-stand
objects.desc: A tall brass hat-stand that normally stands in the corner of Silas's vestry office.

objects.name: Bank statements
objects.desc: Edmund's own copies of the estate bank statements, kept in the study strongbox.

objects.name: Desk blotter
objects.desc: The green blotting pad on Edmund's study desk.

objects.name: Rowan's green coat
objects.desc: The groundskeeper's heavy green work coat.

objects.name: Dr Marsh's examination notes
objects.desc: Iris's handwritten notes on Edmund's injuries, kept for the coroner.

attitudes.content: He has been drawing money from the Vale estate accounts for two years.
To go through the estate ledger himself tonight and question the figures.
Edmund's audit will expose the embezzlement and ruin him.
To silence Edmund before he can take the ledger to anyone.
To be seen working late at his vestry office as usual.
To get away from the manor after a sharp word with Edmund over household money.
To return home and retire for the night.
To keep the inn open and serve her customers through the evening.
To finish potting and repairing frames in the greenhouse.
To attend patients: first at the surgery, then Rowan's cut hand when sent for.
To walk his evening round of the square.
To take Edmund his morning tea as she always does.
To examine Edmund's body when called to the manor.
To keep her quarrel with Edmund private, so she avoids admitting she left the manor that evening.
To keep a patient's treatment confidential unless it is already plainly known.
To leave a figure in his lit vestry window so anyone passing thinks he is still at his desk.
The still figure in the lamplit vestry window was Silas Voss working late.
To take the bank statements Edmund locked in the strongbox and lock it again so nothing looks disturbed.
With his bloodied coat and cut hand, the village will say it is Edmund's blood on him.
To scrub his own blood out of the coat cuff before anyone asks, and say nothing of it.
To keep her examination findings for the coroner, showing them only to someone plainly acting for the constable.
To ask Mrs Finch to say nothing of her supper at the Rook, so no one asks why she left the manor.
To keep Miss Vale's evening to herself as asked, unless it is plainly known already.
Having asked Mrs Finch for silence, to speak only of what she herself saw at the Rook, never for Mrs Finch.

events.summary: Edmund works through the estate ledger in his study.
Silas works at his vestry office, lamp lit.
Silas strikes Edmund with the brass paperweight in the study.
Silas returns to the vestry, puts the hat-stand back in its corner and stays late.
Clara attends to household matters, quarrels briefly with Edmund over money.
Clara takes supper by the inn fire, served by Ada.
Clara returns to the manor and retires without entering the study.
Ada runs the bar and dining room all evening.
Rowan repairs frames in the greenhouse.
A cracked pane gives way and gashes Rowan's left hand.
Iris sees evening patients at her surgery.
Iris stitches and bandages Rowan's hand at the greenhouse.
Rowan rests in the greenhouse bothy.
Iris returns to the surgery and writes up her notes.
Bell walks his round of the square.
Clara brings morning tea and finds Edmund dead in the study.
Iris examines Edmund's body in the study.
Ada pencils Miss Vale's supper bill, takes payment and spikes it behind the bar.
Silas moves the hat-stand to the lit window, hangs his coat and hat on it, and slips out.
On his round Bell twice looks across at the lit vestry window and sees a still, hunched shape.
Silas opens the study strongbox with his own key, takes Edmund's bank statements, and locks it again.
Hearing of the death, Rowan soaks and scrubs the bloodied cuff of his green coat in the bothy.
Back at her surgery, Iris writes up her examination of Edmund's injuries for the coroner.
Early morning, Clara slips into the Rook and quietly asks Ada to keep her supper there to herself.
After Clara leaves, Ada takes Miss Vale's slip off the spike and tucks it under the cash box.
Rowan tips the bloody lint from the bothy bin onto the compost heap, covers it, and rinses the bin.
Rowan takes his bloodied coat off the greenhouse-door peg, wets it at the tap and carries it dripping to the bothy.

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased, Edmund Vale, reveals a single heavy blow to the back of the head, causing significant skull trauma. The wound pattern suggests a hard, blunt object was used with considerable force. Death occurred between half past nine and ten o'clock, and there are no other marks of violence upon the body.
signs.show: I've examined Mr Vale's body, and he died from a heavy blow to the back of the head between half past nine and ten o'clock last night. Did you see or hear anything in that time?

reactions.silas: A grim business, Inspector. I was at my desk in the vestry through that hour, lamp lit, as anyone passing would attest — I certainly cannot account for what befell poor Edmund at his home.

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: He died between half past nine and ten o'clock, from a heavy blow to the back of the head — struck once, and struck hard, poor man.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Edmund?
signs.show: Dr Marsh tells me Mr Vale died from a heavy blow to the back of the head with a blunt object, sometime between half past nine and ten last night. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me he died from a blow to the back of the head between half past nine and ten last night. Is that your full assessment?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: Walking my round of the square, same as every night. Saw the vestry window lit up, Voss hunched over his work as usual, nothing amiss that I could see.
signs.confront: You told me you saw Mr Voss hunched over his work in the vestry window, nothing amiss. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he saw Silas Voss hunched over his work in the lit vestry window on his round, nothing amiss. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I was about my usual rounds — seeing patients at the surgery of an evening, then called out to tend a hand injury, and back to write up my notes after. Nothing out of the ordinary.
signs.confront: You told me you saw patients, were called out for a hand injury, then went back to write up your notes. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was doing her usual evening rounds, was called out to tend a hand injury, then went back to write up her notes. Does that sound right to you?

signs.speaker: ada
signs.title: Ada Finch on the evening
signs.text: Oh, it was the usual busy evening here, love, bar and dining room both going full tilt. I had someone in for supper by the fire, but I don't like to natter about who eats what, do I?
signs.confront: You told me it was a busy night and someone was in for supper by the fire, but you wouldn't say who. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says it was a busy night at the inn with someone in for supper by the fire, though she won't say who. Can you tell me anything more about that?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: I had words with Edmund over money, then went out for a while before retiring. I came straight home after and went to bed without disturbing the study.
signs.confront: You told me you argued with Edmund, went out, then came straight home and went to bed without disturbing the study. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she argued with Edmund about money, went out for a while, then came straight home and went to bed without disturbing the study. Do you know if that's true?

signs.speaker: silas
signs.title: Silas Voss on the evening
signs.text: I was at my vestry office, working late by lamplight, as I often do. I saw to some papers and stayed at my desk most of the night.
signs.confront: You told me you were at your desk in the vestry working on papers most of the night. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Voss says he was at his vestry office working late by lamplight, seeing to papers most of the night. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the evening
signs.text: Cut my hand on a cracked pane, working late in the greenhouse. Iris patched it up for me. Spent the rest of the night resting in the bothy, nowhere else.
signs.confront: You told me you cut your hand, were patched up by Dr Marsh, then stayed in the bothy the rest of the night. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says he cut his hand on a cracked pane in the greenhouse, was patched up by Dr Marsh, then rested in the bothy the rest of the night. Do you know if that's so?

signs.title: Dr Marsh on the greenhouse call
signs.text: "I got to the greenhouse at ten to nine. Mr Pike had a deep cut across the left palm, glass. Seven stitches. I didn't leave until ten past ten. He was sitting in front of me the whole time."
signs.speaker: iris
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh won't discuss a patient at first. Shown her own dressings and wrapper from the compost heap behind Rowan's greenhouse, she accepts that the visit is already known and gives the times.
signs.ask: Dr Marsh, what happened when you were called to the greenhouse?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she treated Mr Pike's cut hand in the greenhouse from ten to nine until ten past ten, and that he sat before her the whole time. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you treated my cut hand from ten to nine until ten past ten, and that I sat in front of you the whole time. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.rowan: Aye, that's right. Cut myself on a cracked pane, glass right through the palm. Doctor sat with me the whole time seeing to it — nothing more to it than that.

signs.direct: Dr Marsh says you came in with a deep glass cut to your palm just before nine, needed seven stitches, and sat before her until past ten. Is that so?

signs.title: Mrs Finch on last night's supper
signs.text: "Miss Vale? Came in on the stroke of nine, she did, took the seat by the fire and had the chop and a glass of cider. Barely said two words, poor lamb. Didn't stir till gone half ten, I'd swear to it, I was up and down to her table all night."
signs.speaker: ada
signs.unlock: Clara asked Mrs Finch to keep quiet. Once you show her Miss Vale's settled bill from under her own cash box, she sees the visit is known already and has no reason left to stay quiet.
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, what can you tell me about last night's supper trade?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says Miss Vale sat by the fire from nine till half past ten, barely spoke, and never left her table. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me I sat by your fire from nine till half past ten and never left my table. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.clara: That's so. I took supper alone by the fire, as she says. I'd nothing to add to it.

signs.direct: Mrs Finch says you arrived at nine, ate by the fire, and didn't leave your table until gone half ten. Does that match what you remember?

signs.title: Miss Vale on the inn
signs.text: "I was on the settle by the fire at the Rook from nine until half past ten. I kept my eyes on the room. I didn't wish to be spoken to. The landlady came and went behind the bar, and to my table. She was never out of my sight long."
signs.speaker: clara
signs.unlock: Once she sees her own settled bill from the Rook, Clara can no longer pretend she stayed home that evening. She gives up her reserve and says where she was, and who was there.
signs.reading: From the settle every way out of the Rook's room is in view. If Mrs Finch was never out of Miss Vale's sight for long, she never left the inn.
signs.ask: Miss Vale, what happened when you visited the inn last night?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she sat on the settle by the fire at the Rook from nine until half past ten and kept the landlady in sight the whole time. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you sat by the fire from nine until half past ten and kept me in sight the whole time. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.ada: Well, that's about the shape of it, though I do have my customers to see to, so I can't say I never took my eyes off her table. But she was there right enough, all evening.

concede.s_settle_view: Yes, that settle sees the whole bar and the only way to the yard, so Mrs Finch was there, nine until half past ten, just as I said. I named no one because I did not think it my place, only my eyes'.

signs.direct: Miss Vale says she watched you come and go from behind the bar to her table the whole evening, and that she never lost sight of you long. Is that so?

signs.title: A slip under the cash box
signs.text: The spike behind the bar holds last night's slips, but one is missing from the run. Tucked flat beneath the cash box under the bar is a pencilled slip: 'Miss Vale. Chop, cider. 1s 9d. Pd.'
signs.unlock: Mrs Finch's nervous glance at the cash box under the bar tells you where to look when she turns away to serve.
signs.show: There's a supper slip tucked flat beneath the cash box, marked for Miss Vale's chop and cider, paid, though it's missing from the spike where the others are kept. Can you explain why it was hidden there?

reactions.ada: Oh! Well now, that's Miss Vale's, right enough — chop and cider, paid fair and square. I tucked it away 'cos she asked me kindly to keep her supper quiet, and I'm not one to break a promise to a lady, clue or no clue.

signs.direct: I found a pencilled slip under the cash box here, charging you for a chop and cider, marked paid. Were you here that evening?

signs.title: The compost heap
signs.text: The tin bin in the bothy stands empty and freshly rinsed. On the compost heap behind the greenhouse, under a forkful of new leaf mould: blood-soaked lint, a few snipped ends of suture silk, and a torn paper wrapper printed 'Dr I. Marsh, Bellweather'.
signs.unlock: The bucket and carbolic show Mr Pike has been cleaning this morning, so you check what else he has cleaned. The rinsed bin sends you to the freshly turned compost heap.
signs.show: The tin bin in the bothy's been rinsed clean, but I found blood-soaked lint, snipped suture silk, and a torn wrapper marked 'Dr I. Marsh' buried in the compost heap. Can you tell me who's been using that heap?

reactions.rowan: That's off my hand, not his. Cut it on a pane, doctor stitched it, and I put the mess where it belongs — on the heap. Nothing more to it.

signs.direct: I found lint, suture silk, and a torn wrapper bearing your name buried in the compost behind the greenhouse. Can you explain how they came to be there?

signs.title: Constable Bell on the vestry window
signs.text: "Looked across at the vestry twice on my round. Twenty past nine, then again at ten. Lamp lit, Mr Voss in the window over his papers, head down. Never moved either time. Works too hard, that one."
signs.speaker: bell
signs.ask: Constable Bell, what did you notice about the vestry window?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he looked at the vestry window twice, at twenty past nine and again at ten, and both times saw Mr Voss at his desk with his head down, never moving. Does that match what you recall?
signs.confront: You told me you saw Mr Voss at his desk, unmoving, at twenty past nine and again at ten. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.silas: Working too hard is rather the nature of an audit season, Constable. I've the papers to prove it, if the detective wishes to see how the hours were spent. As for not moving — a man bent over ledgers rarely does.

signs.direct: Constable Bell says he saw you twice at the vestry window, head down over your papers, never moving. Is that so?

signs.title: Rings in the dust
signs.text: The brass hat-stand is back in its corner in the vestry office. Its three feet sit a little off their own dusty rings. By the window, beside the desk chair, three matching rings show clean in the dust on the boards. A grey wool thread is caught on a hook of the stand.
signs.unlock: The constable's account of a figure in one particular window tells you which part of the vestry office to look at closely.
signs.reading: The stand was recently set just where Bell saw his motionless 'figure'. Hung with a coat and hat against the lamp, it would look from the square like a man bent over his desk.
signs.show: The hat-stand in the vestry office has moved—there are clean rings in the dust by the desk chair that don't match where it stands now, and a grey thread's caught on its hook. Do you know why it was shifted?

reactions.silas: The hat-stand does move about the office from time to time — I shift it when I'm tidying papers by the window. I fail to see what dust rings prove.
reactions.bell: Well now. If the hat-stand was stood by that window, then what I took for Mr Voss hunched over his papers might've been nowt but that stand and a coat on it. I called it as I saw it, mind — a still shape in a lit window, twice over. Didn't think to doubt me own eyes.

signs.title: Miss Vale on the strongbox
signs.text: "The strongbox? There were only ever two keys. Edmund's stayed on his watch chain. The other one Mr Voss kept, for the estate papers."
signs.speaker: clara
signs.unlock: Once she has told you all about her evening at the Rook, Clara stops guarding the family's affairs and answers your questions about the study.
signs.show: You've told me there were only ever two keys to the strongbox - Edmund's on his watch chain, and the other kept by Mr Voss for the estate papers. Is that correct?

reactions.silas: That is correct. I have always held the second key, for the estate papers — quite properly, as Edmund's solicitor.

signs.title: The study strongbox
signs.text: The strongbox under the study desk is locked. Its lock shows no scratches and the lid has not been forced. Inside, a folder marked 'Bank' is empty. Edmund's strongbox key still hangs on his watch chain.
signs.reading: The box was opened without force and locked again, and Edmund's key never left his chain. So whoever emptied the folder used the only other key.
signs.show: The study strongbox is locked with no scratches or forcing, but the folder marked 'Bank' inside is empty, and Edmund's key is still on his watch chain. Do you know what became of what was in that folder?

reactions.silas: The strongbox was locked when I left it, as it should be. I have no explanation for an empty folder beyond what the bank itself can tell you.

signs.title: The study blotter
signs.text: Held up to a mirror, the fresh pencil marks pressed into the blotter read: 'S.V. — Mar. £40, Jun. £55, Sept. £60 — drawn, no receipts. Bank shows his signature. Ask him.'
signs.unlock: After admitting the quarrel, Clara says Edmund sat writing figures at his desk all evening and points you to the blotter he always pressed his notes on.
signs.show: The pressed marks on the study blotter show sums drawn against your initials in March, June, and September, with no receipts, and a note to check the bank signature against yours. Can you explain these withdrawals?

reactions.silas: Pencil impressions prove nothing but that someone wrote figures near my initials. I manage estate accounts for many clients, Inspector; draw your own conclusions carefully.

signs.direct: The blotter here carries pressed marks noting sums drawn by you in March, June, and September, with no receipts, and a note questioning your signature at the bank. Can you explain this?

signs.title: A coat in the bucket
signs.text: In the bothy a green work coat is pushed down in a bucket of pink-tinged water, carbolic soap beside it. Mr Pike stands in front of the bucket. "Just mucky. Leave it." He does not meet your eye.
signs.unlock: You follow the pink drips from the empty peg to the bothy door, and find Mr Pike standing over his bucket.
signs.show: Mr Pike is scrubbing his green work coat in a bucket of pink-tinged water with carbolic soap, and won't meet my eye about it. Can you tell me why he's washing it?
signs.confront: You're scrubbing your coat in pink water and won't meet my eye. Why are you washing it?

reactions.rowan: Told you. Mucky, that's all. Leave it be — it's my coat, my business.

signs.direct: You have a green work coat pushed down in a bucket of pink-tinged water with carbolic soap beside it, and you told me to leave it, calling it just mucky. Is that so?

signs.title: Mr Pike on the coat
signs.text: "All right. That's my blood. Pane went at eight, caught my palm, I held the cuff to it till the doctor came. Folk were already on about my hand and my coat. When I heard about Mr Vale I thought they'd say it was his. So I scrubbed it. Stupid."
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.unlock: Once you tell him Dr Marsh has already given the times of her visit, Rowan stops thinking his cut will be held against him and explains the coat.
signs.ask: Mr Pike, what happened at the greenhouse last night involving your coat?
signs.show: Mr Pike has told me the blood on his coat was his own, from a pane cutting his palm at eight o'clock, and that he scrubbed it clean once talk turned to Mr Vale. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You've told me the blood was your own, from the pane cutting your hand at eight, and that you scrubbed the coat once people started talking about Mr Vale. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: Dr Marsh's notes for the coroner
signs.text: In a neat clinical hand: 'E. Vale. Single depressed fracture, right temple, edge matches base of brass paperweight. No wound behind. Bruising on both forearms at the front, as if raised against someone facing him. Struck from in front, at close quarters, across the desk. Death within minutes.'
signs.unlock: Once she has told you about her greenhouse visit, Dr Marsh accepts that you are acting for Constable Bell. She takes her coroner's notes from the drawer and lets you read them.
signs.reading: Edmund was facing his attacker when the blow landed on his right temple. By the rule, a swing that lands on the right side of someone facing you comes from the left hand.
signs.show: Dr Marsh's notes say Vale was struck once from the front at close range, with bruising on his forearms as if he'd raised them against someone facing him. Does that match what you saw?

reactions.iris: That's my own hand and my own findings, written for the coroner as they should be. I'll say no more than what's there until he calls for it.
reactions.silas: A distressing account, but a medical matter, not a legal one. I can offer no insight into how Edmund met his end.

signs.title: Mrs Finch goes quiet
signs.text: Mrs Finch will talk about anyone else's evening, but when Miss Vale comes up she starts wiping a clean glass. "Oh, I couldn't rightly say, dear, it was that busy." Her eyes flick to the cash box under the bar and then away.
signs.show: Mrs Finch goes quiet and starts wiping a clean glass whenever Miss Vale is mentioned, her eyes flicking to the cash box under the bar. Do you know why she's so reluctant to speak on it?
signs.confront: You go quiet and start wiping a glass whenever Miss Vale comes up, glancing at the cash box. Why are you so reluctant to speak on it?

reactions.ada: Oh, you noticed that, did you — well, a lady asked for her privacy and I'm not one to gossip about her supper, that's all it is, dear.
reactions.clara: Mrs Finch was only being kind. I asked her to keep my supper to herself, and I'd rather not say more than that — it's a private matter, nothing to do with Edmund.

signs.direct: You go quiet and start wiping a clean glass whenever Miss Vale is mentioned, and your eyes flick to the cash box under the bar. Is that so?

signs.title: The settle by the fire
signs.text: Mrs Finch shows you the high-backed settle by the Rook's fire where Miss Vale sat. From it you can see the whole bar, the street door, and the only passage to the kitchen and yard. There is no other way out of the room.
signs.unlock: Once she's talking about Miss Vale's supper, Mrs Finch takes you over to the seat by the fire and shows you where Miss Vale sat.
signs.show: From the settle by the fire you can see the whole bar, the street door, and the only passage to the kitchen and yard, with no other way out. Does that match what you recall of the room that night?

signs.title: An empty peg
signs.text: The peg by the greenhouse door, where Mr Pike's work coat usually hangs, is empty. Pinkish drips run from the tap across the brick path and stop at the bothy door.
signs.show: The peg by the greenhouse door where your coat usually hangs is empty, and there are pinkish drips running from the tap along the brick path to the bothy door. Can you tell me what happened there?

reactions.rowan: Coat's soaking, told you that. Tap's there for washing up, drips go where they go. Nothing sinister in it.

signs.direct: The peg where your work coat usually hangs is empty, and pinkish drips lead from the tap along the brick path to the bothy door. Can you tell me where your coat is and what those drips are?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.unlock: once you have A slip under the cash box, you can ask Clara Vale about it
signs.title: Clara Vale on a slip under the cash box
signs.text: I simply asked Ada to keep my supper bill to herself rather than leaving it out for anyone to see — a lady's accounts are her own business, Constable.
signs.ask: Ada has a slip here for your supper, tucked under the cash box rather than on the spike as usual. Can you explain that?
signs.show: Clara Vale says she only asked Ada to keep her supper bill private, not leave it lying out. Do you know anything about that arrangement?
signs.confront: You told me you only asked Ada to keep your supper bill private, not leave it out for anyone to see. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: A ledger tucked in the vestry desk
signs.text: 'Estate of Vale — advances to self, Mar/Jun/Sept, to be repaid before audit. If E.V. insists on going through the books himself, all is lost.' The hand is Silas Voss's own, dated some weeks past.
signs.unlock: once you have the study blotter, you know what to ask
signs.show: I found a ledger hidden in the vestry desk, written in Silas Voss's own hand, listing advances he took from the Vale estate to be repaid before any audit. Did you know Voss was helping himself to the estate's funds?
signs.direct: I found a ledger in your hand, speaking of advances to yourself to be repaid before audit, and warning that all would be lost if Edmund went through the books himself. Can you explain this?

title: The Study Door
synopsis: Edmund Vale is found dead in his study at Vale Manor.

clara: I manage the day-to-day running of Vale Manor, seeing to the household accounts and staff.
Edmund was my brother, and I've lived at the manor with him for years.
I keep to the family wing of the manor, where my own things are kept.
I've known Ada, Rowan, Silas, Iris and Constable Bell for years, as everyone in the village does.
This morning I brought Edmund his tea as I always do and found him dead in the study, which is how the alarm was raised.
rowan: I'm the groundskeeper at Vale Manor, and I look after the greenhouse and grounds.
I've worked for the Vale family for years, so I know Clara and Edmund well from my daily work.
Everyone in the village has noticed my bandaged hand and been asking after it this morning.
silas: I'm the estate solicitor, and I keep an office in the vestry where I handle Edmund's accounts and paperwork.
I've managed the Vale family's legal and financial affairs for a long time, so I know Clara and Edmund well.
I live and work mostly out of the vestry, where my papers and ledgers are kept.
The whole village is talking this morning about Edmund's death and Clara finding him.
ada: I run the Rook & Lantern, the village inn, tending bar and seeing to guests.
I live at the inn and keep the till and my papers behind the bar.
I've known everyone in the village for years through the inn trade, including Clara, Rowan and Silas.
iris: I know the Vale family well, having attended to them over the years.
I keep my medical instruments and notes at the surgery.
I was sent for this morning to examine Edmund's body in the study after Clara found him.
I know Rowan because I often treat small injuries he gets about the grounds.
bell: I'm the village constable, and my rounds take me around the square and the main buildings each evening.
I know everyone in the village by name and habit, from years of keeping the peace here.
I secured the manor this morning once word came that Edmund was found dead.
I keep no personal keys to the manor or vestry, only my usual keys to the lock-up on the square.

moods.iris: Businesslike but heavy-hearted, mindful of keeping her patients' and findings' details to herself.
